catalog_quote: En la mayoría de las variedades centrales del quechua, el acento se asigna a la penúltima sílaba. Por ejemplo: [aywáːpis] /aywa-ː-pis/ ‘yo también voy’ [aywašaːpíta] /aywa-ša-ː-pita/ ‘desde que fui’. En esos dialectos, la vocal larga que funciona como marcador de primera persona se acentúa cuando está en posición final de palabra: [aywáː] /aywa-ː/ ‘voy’. En la variedad del Huallaga y algunas otras variedades, también se acentúan las vocales largas finales que tienen otra procedencia: [manárax̥] ~ [manaráː] /mana-raq/ ‘todavía no’ [aywášax̥] ~ [aywašáː] /aywa-šaq/ ‘iré’. Según el análisis Vː = [V][V], la regla de colocación del acento podría formularse así: “Acentúese la penúltima vocal”. ... En todo caso, los últimos dos ejemplos muestran que, para estas variedades la colocación del acento es una regla que no trata a las palabras que terminan en vocal larga como a las que terminan en consonante. [Toliver 2008b:52] Se puede saber que en el segundo caso la partícula es ligada por la colocación de la fuerza de la voz que en quechua recae en la penúltima sílaba: a.'li.cag NO 'a.li # cag

Por ejemplo: [aywáːpis] /aywa-ː-pis/ ‘yo también voy’, [aywašaːpíta] /aywa-ša-ː-pita/ ‘desde que fui’. new_statements.translation: In most of the central varieties of Quechua, stress is assigned to the penultimate syllable, e.g. [aywáːpis] 'I also go', [aywašaːpíta] 'since I went'. In those dialects, the long vowel that functions as first-person marker is stressed when it is word-final: [aywáː] 'I go'. In the Huallaga variety and some other varieties, final long vowels of other origins are also stressed: [manáraχ ~ manaráː] 'not yet', [aywášaχ ~ aywašáː] 'I will go'.
new_statements.citation: Weber, David J. & Peter N. Landerman. 2008. La interpretación de las vocales largas en el quechua. In Heidi Coombs & Ågot Bergli (eds.), Estudios quechuas II (Serie Lingüística Peruana 55), 12-28. Lima: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano. [Areal statement for Central Quechua; corroborated in the same volume by Ralph Toliver (SIL linguist for Pasco Quechua), 'Procesos de préstamo y el proceso de afecto en sobrenombres de quechua', p.52: 'la colocación de la fuerza de la voz que en quechua recae en la penúltima sílaba: a.ˈli.cag, NO ˈa.li # cag'.]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress on the penultimate syllable; a word-final long vowel (at least the 1st-person length morpheme) attracts stress to the final syllable. This is stated for 'most Central Quechua varieties' (Quechua I, which includes the Yaru group to which Chaupihuaranga belongs), not verified specifically for Chaupihuaranga in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final long vowels are stressed (1st-person marker everywhere; other final long vowels in Huallaga 'and some other varieties'); some Ancash varieties instead have initial stress with utterance-final stress on the last heavy syllable (Parker 1976:58) — Ancash is outside Yaru.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule; Toliver's p.52 remark uses stress placement (a.'li.cag) as a diagnostic that cag has become a bound form, i.e. the domain is the phonological word including enclitic-like elements. Neither statement is based on Chaupihuaranga data specifically: Weber & Landerman speak of Central Quechua generally (examples in Huallaga-type transcription); Toliver's article data are mainly Ambo-Pasco, Margos-Yarowilca-Lauricocha and Huamalíes (p.50).
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog yana1272 'Chaupihuaranga Quechua' = ISO qur (Yanahuanca Pasco) plus dialect nodes carr1251 (Carrión) and sant1433 (Santa Ana de Tusi, ISO qxt). The one dedicated phonology (Escobar 1967) describes Yanacocha, a community in Yanahuanca district (core Chaupihuaranga). Creider 1967 'Picoy', which Glottolog also files under yana1272, describes Picoy in Santa Leonor district, Huaura, Lima — a Lima Yaru lect, not Chaupihuaranga. The stress statement quoted here is areal (Central Quechua / 'quechua' generally) from SIL linguists working in Huánuco-Pasco, not a Chaupihuaranga-specific description; Toliver's own data are mainly Ambo-Pasco (qva, ambo1251), Margos-Yarowilca-Lauricocha and Huamalíes.

new_statements.quote: In most Quechua dialects stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel of each polysyllabic word form [...]. In Tarma and the dialect of northern Junin word-final stress can occur as a result of the elision of a final syllable. [...] In the Quechua I dialects stress is maintained in word-final position when the long vowel morpheme referring to first-person subject or possessor is immediately followed by a word boundary [...] Otherwise, penultimate stress is predominant. More complex, non-penultimate stress patterns, involving word-initial stress and stress dependent on syllable structure, are found in QI Ancash and in QI Cajatambo (cf. Torero 1964: 461; Parker 1976).

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Weber & Landerman 2008 statement (penultimate stress in the central varieties, with the word-final first-person long vowel stressed). It also refines: Tarma/northern Junín elision-induced final stress, interjections, and it explicitly localises the non-penultimate systems to Ancash and Cajatambo, so Pasco/Yaru falls under the default. The book never names Chaupihuaranga (0 full-text hits) and mentions 'Yaru' only in the dialect classification (index pp. 185, 193), so the statement is a family-level generalisation covering Quechua I rather than a description of this lect. Note: the archive.org item is controlled-lending with the text private (401), the WALS ope…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress on the penultimate vowel of every polysyllabic word in most Quechua dialects; in the Quechua I (central) dialects, to which the Yaru/Pasco group containing Chaupihuaranga belongs, a word-final first-person long vowel (-: 'I / my') keeps the stress in final position; otherwise penultimate stress predominates. Word-final stress also arises in interjections and, in Tarma and northern Junín (Yaru dialects), from elision of a final syllable. The non-penultimate systems (initial stress, syllable-structure-sensitive stress) are confined to quantity-insensitive Ancash and quantity-insensitive Cajatambo, i.e. not Pasco; Pacaraos (phonemic final vs penultimate) is a separate case.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the recovered passage.
new_statements.exceptions: Interjections and emphatic expressions (alalaw 'how cold!') word-final; elision of a final syllable in Tarma and northern Junín (aywa-mu-ra-ygi ~ aywa-mu-ra-y); the first-person long-vowel morpheme word-finally attracts stress in quantity-insensitive dialects; quantity-insensitive Ancash and quantity-insensitive Cajatambo have word-initial and syllable-structure-dependent stress; Pacaraos has phonemic penultimate/final stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Adelaar & Muysken describe Quechua I as a whole; the dialect-specific remarks are about Tarma and northern Junín (Yaru group, neighbouring Chaupihuaranga in Pasco), Ancash, Cajatambo and Pacaraos, not Chaupihuaranga/Yanacocha itself. Chaupihuaranga is not named anywhere in the book's searchable text.
